sentences.text: Last time, a single count ran as 2 jobs and 2 stages.
Here's a new question for our cast: how many higher-risk patients does each clinic have?
One action answers it. Spark ran it as 2 jobs, 2 stages and 5 tasks.
Where do those numbers come from?
Welcome to Spark, Visually.
Today: cut at the walls.
Line one is last episode's filter. Line two asks for a count per clinic, and the driver adds it to the plan.
Nothing has run yet. But this step is different.
A clinic's patients sit in different piles. So when it runs, Spark counts in two steps.
First, each pile counts its own patients, clinic by clinic. Then those partial counts must meet, so each clinic's numbers move to one place. That step is an exchange.
Spark cuts the plan at every exchange, and each piece is a stage.
Stage one reads, filters and counts each pile. Stage two finishes the counts.
Between the two stands a wall: nothing beyond it starts until everything before it has finished.
Stage two can't start early, because it needs a piece from every pile.
Inside a stage, the work is split one task per pile. Four piles, so stage one runs 4 tasks.
Line three is the action. Four tasks go down and run side by side.
Each one finishes when its own pile is done, and stage two can't begin until the last one does.
When the last one finishes, the wall opens. The partial counts cross, and stage two adds them up.
Alder has 6 higher-risk patients, Birch 24, Cedar 10 and Dune 6. Elm has none, so it gets no row at all.
And stage two's tasks? The exchange deals into 200 piles by default. These are tiny, so Spark merges them into one: one pile, one task.
Four tasks, then one: those are our 5.
Line four prints the plan Spark ran. Read it from the bottom up: the scan, the filter, the partial count.
Then a line that starts with Exchange. That's the wall, and the 200 piles it deals into.
Beside the steps sit star-one and star-two. They aren't stage numbers: they number the chains of steps Spark compiles into one function.
Adaptive execution counts its query stages, 0 and 1, its own way too.
Spark's UI numbered our two stages 2 and 4.
One catch: on Spark Connect, which some Databricks compute uses, explain() shows the starting plan, even after the run.
To see the plan that ran, use the Spark UI, or the query profile.
Now, why two jobs? With adaptive execution on, as it is by default, Spark runs stage one as a job of its own.
It looks at how much stage one actually wrote, and only then plans the rest. That's episode 12.
The second job lists that first stage again, marked skipped. Its work was done, and its output was still there to reuse.
The skipped copy even took a number of its own: 3.
Switch adaptive execution off and count again, and you get 1 job with the same two stages. But now stage two runs 200 tasks, one per pile, and most of those piles are empty.
One last line: join the cast to a small table of clinics.
Spark would normally take a shortcut with a table this small, and the hint asks it not to. That's episode 8.
So both sides are dealt out by clinic: each side gets its own stage, and a third stage joins them.
Neither input needs the other, so there's no wall between them, and they run at the same time.
One line of code, three stages: a stage isn't a line of code.
Let's gather it up.
An action starts one job or several, and adaptive execution is one reason for several. Spark cuts its plan at every exchange, and each piece is a stage.
A stage runs one task per pile, and a wall stands wherever one stage needs another's output.
But what exactly crosses the wall? Next time: everyone sends to everyone.
This has been Spark, Visually. Thanks for watching the cluster with us.
